summary: Intro demo of Redwood's hosted chat API focused on streaming behaviour, parameter tuning, retry/backoff patterns, and how different params affect token cost. Customer was evaluating fast checkout assistant; concerns: tail latency, cost per session, and data residency. Agreed on a short baseline and to share pricing + security docs.
topics: Streaming mechanics (how streaming chunks map to tokens and latency)
Generation params: temperature, max_tokens, stop, top_p, presence/penalty tradeoffs
Retries and idempotency: backoff patterns and client-side best practices
Console Optimize suggestions: batching, prefix caching, quantization recommendations
Security brief: data retention, SOC2, VPC/private options (high level)
transcript: [00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Leo, our SE. We'll keep this to ~40 minutes and then cover next steps.

[00:12] Jamal Reed: Cool thanks, quick note — we're trying to replace a lambda-based microservice that does customer checkout suggestions, latency target is sub-300ms 95th pct on the interactive path.
[00:25] Leo Martinez: got it. we'll demo hosted chat, show streaming behavior, and how params affect cost and latency. if we need, we can talk Dedicated later.
[00:38] Sofia Morales: also we have strict logging rules — audit logs, can't send raw PII offsite without a contract. curious how redwood handles retention.
[00:50] Maya Patel: yes we'll flag security later. quick agenda, live demo of streaming, then param walkthrough, retry patterns, and cost/console tips. sound ok?
[01:05] Evan Li: yep that's perfect

[02:02] Leo Martinez: starting the demo — pulling up a basic chat request in the console. note: streaming is enabled by default on chat endpoint; you get partial deltas as tokens are generated. sometimes transcripts will show short chunks every 200ms depending on tokenization.

[02:34] [screen share noise] Leo Martinez: here's a sample prompt for checkout assistance. we're using the 'small-rl' family for demo — in production you'd pick a model balancing cost and quality. temperature 0.2, max_tokens 150.
[03:10] Sofia Morales: small-rl — is that quantized? how's memory footprint?

[03:18] Leo Martinez: it's a quant-friendly variant, yes. memory summary in console Optimize tab recommends a 4-bit qprofile for throughput. that saves tokens? no, sorry that saves GPU memory/cost not token units — my bad, mixing terms.
[03:42] Jamal Reed: when you say streaming chunks — do we get full sentences or token deltas? we worried about partial words showing up in UI.

[03:55] Leo Martinez: you get token-level deltas. UI can buffer until whitespace or punctuation, but client decides. if you prefer sentence-level, do a short debounce client-side. that also reduces re-renders and perceived flicker.
[04:20] [background chatter] Evan Li: and cost implications? more streaming messages == more billable tokens?

[04:30] Maya Patel: billing is per generated token + input tokens. streaming only affects network events, not billing. but how you set max_tokens and stop sequences directly affects token counts and cost per session.

[05:12] Leo Martinez: demo: toggling max_tokens from 150 to 80 — you'll see latency hardly changes for prefix steps but total token cost drops — we recommend setting conservative max_tokens plus a clear stop token to prevent runaway generations.
[06:05] Sofia Morales: what's a safe retry strategy for idempotency? if we get a transient 503 mid-stream, should the client retry from scratch?

[06:18] Leo Martinez: good Q. best practice: make generation idempotent by client-side request IDs, and on server-side use prefix caching so we can resume from last known KV state. but note: hosted resume requires using the conversation endpoint with streaming resume support; otherwise restart and dedupe on client.
[06:45] Jamal Reed: you mentioned KV cache — I'm reading that as K V cash sometimes in logs — what is that?

[06:55] Leo Martinez: ha — sorry, it's KV cache (key-value), stores past tokens / attention cache to speed autoregressive decoding on subsequent requests. it reduces latency on follow-up messages and lowers GPU work.
[07:30] [crosstalk] Sofia Morales: does that cache persist across model versions?

[07:38] Leo Martinez: generally per model-version; when you roll a model, cache is invalidated. Console shows cache hit rates in per-route dashboard so you can tune conversation length and caching strategy.

[08:05] Maya Patel: jumping to retry patterns — typical client approach is exponential backoff with jitter, 3 total attempts for idempotent operations. for non-idempotent, use server fallbacks instead of retries.
[08:30] Jamal Reed: any canned client code you share?
[08:36] Maya Patel: yes, we'll send a node/python snippet that implements idempotency keys and backoff. Leo will attach it to the follow-up notes.

[09:10] Leo Martinez: quick show of console Optimize — it analyzes your route and suggests batching, prefix caching, and quantization profiles. for chat-heavy workloads we often recommend small-batch sizes to preserve latency while using cache aggressively.
[09:48] Evan Li: batching seems at odds with our latency SLO. how do you balance that?

[09:55] Leo Martinez: use adaptive batching: route-level config that expands batching during low concurrency, and drops to single request when latency must be low. Optimize will propose a batch-window and expected latency tradeoff.

[10:40] [30 sec pause while Leo pulls logs] Leo Martinez: here's a simple chart — 95th pctl drops from 480ms to 320ms with prefix caching and same req rate. couple caveats: cold-starts and very long contexts still hit tails.
[11:10] Sofia Morales: context length — we have multi-turn carts with 30 messages; do you recommend trimming history?

[11:18] Leo Martinez: yes, you can summarize earlier turns or use selective context (only last N messages). Console has a 'context summarizer' helper template that creates a compressed summary to keep effective context small.
[12:05] Jamal Reed: security quick question — where do logs live? we need auditability and to control retention.

[12:12] Maya Patel: hosted stores logs per account; retention configurable. we have SOC 2 and enterprise contracts allow custom retention and optional VPC/private deployment for stricter cases. we'll share the SOC2 summary in follow-up.
[12:45] Evan Li: any issues with sending hashed PII?
[12:51] Leo Martinez: hashed PII is ok, but best practice is to redact sensitive fields before sending. Optimize can help you instrument which prompt tokens account for most of the cost.

[13:30] Leo Martinez: quick live test — I'll purposely trigger a simulated 502 on a stream and show backoff. note the client receives partial tokens up to the failure; client should either display an error or attempt a resume if you support conversation-resume API.

[14:10] [demo noise] Leo Martinez: hitting the 502 now, client got partial output — our recom mendation: if partial output acceptable, show it and then offer retry; if atomic response needed, use idempotent request ids and restart.
[15:05] Sofia Morales: what about rate limits and throttling? we might burst during sales peaks.

[15:12] Maya Patel: hosted has tiered rate limits; Console shows per-route quota. for predictable bursts we recommend Dedicated or reserved burst capacity. Optimize can simulate cost/throughput for projected traffic patterns.
[15:50] Jamal Reed: ok, practical ask — would you run a 1-hour baseline using 1000 representative prompts we provide?
[15:58] Maya Patel: yes, Leo will run the baseline and we'll share the numbers. that will guide Dedicated vs hosted decision.
[17:00] Evan Li: one more on billing — if we lower max_tokens but have more retries, could overall cost increase?

[17:12] Leo Martinez: yes, retries can inflate tokens if you repeat the same prompt. that's why idempotent keys + resume + short backoff window matter. also use stop tokens and conservative max_tokens to limit runaway.
[17:45] Sofia Morales: you mentioned console visibility to token breakdown — can we get per-route per-user breakdown for chargebacks?
[17:53] Maya Patel: yes, Console has token-level drilldowns and you can export per-api-key usage. for chargebacks we recommend per-tenant API keys and tagging in ingested requests.
[18:20] [brief silence] Maya Patel: ok to recap?
[18:25] Jamal Reed: yes please

[18:30] Maya Patel: recap — Leo to run baseline (latency + cost) with your prompts; we'll send pricing + SOC2; we'll include client snippets for idempotency + backoff; and the Optimize quickstart that suggests quantization/batching settings. next sync after baseline results.
[19:05] Evan Li: timeline for baseline?
[19:08] Leo Martinez: I'll run it by 2025-11-10 and share results and a short spreadsheet. Maya will include pricing earlier.
[19:25] Sofia Morales: thanks everyone, that was helpful. we'll redact PII from the sample prompts and upload them.
[19:33] Maya Patel: great, thanks all. I'll follow up with the docs and links. closing now.
